campaigns/home-2026-11-02.title: Control your own narrative
campaigns/home-2026-11-02.stage: Week 1 written in full; weeks 2–4 in outline
campaigns/home-2026-11-02.news: Internal context: Airbnb announced (about 20–21 Oct) that for bookings from 20 November 2026 hosts can't require bigger checkout tasks (stripping beds, washing and putting away dishes, laundry, taking rubbish outside). Small requests stay (plates in the sink, used towels gathered, sorting rubbish into indoor bins). Host fines are banned, and rules show more prominently on listings. Information isn't restricted: hosts can still tell guests anything about their home. Content only hints at the change (a light nod at most, never an explanation of the rule) and never names the platform, uses its logo or its coral colour, or misstates the rule.

weeks.question: Do hosts respond to 'control your own narrative', and does it feel empowering rather than bitter?
Which host stories make guests (and other hosts) care most?
Do hosts get that sharing information (bin day, how things work) beats rules, and that DigiStayBook is where it lives?
Around 20 November, does the guest-facing respect message get shared without backlash?

posts.hook: There's a dent in the doorframe from my son's skateboard. That's not in any listing.
points: Open on small, specific details of a real home, not on the rules
Only a light nod to the moment: hosts feel their say has been taken away
The turn: nobody can take your story; guests who know whose home it is look after it
DigiStayBook: your welcome, your home's story and everything guests need, behind one QR code

full.caption:
There's a dent in the doorframe from my son's skateboard.
The lemon tree out the back was planted the year we bought the place. Help yourself.
Bin day is Tuesday, and the yellow lid is recycling.

None of that is in a listing. All of it is in a home.

Lately a lot of hosts have felt like their say has been taken away. Here's the part nobody can take: your story. Who you are, why this place matters, how it all works.

Guests who know whose home they're in often treat it that way.

Control your own narrative. DigiStayBook puts your welcome, your home's story and everything guests need behind one QR code on the bench.

full.post_title: What's one thing in your welcome note that changed how guests treated your place?
full.caption:
I keep hearing that the small, specific lines do the most, like "Every summer someone forgets their thongs under the deck. They're in the box by the door."

Hosts with one or two places especially: what's the line or habit that actually made a difference for you?

There's a lot of talk about checkout at the moment and I'm not here to add to it. I'm more interested in the part that's always been in our control.

Things I've seen hosts try:

- A welcome note that says who you are, not just the Wi-Fi password
- Meeting guests on arrival, or a short video hello
- Telling the story of the home (who painted the front door yellow, why there's an old fishing rod over the door)
- Writing house info as information, e.g. "collection is Monday, yellow lid is recycling" rather than "take the bins out"
- A guestbook, paper or digital, where past guests leave notes

Does any of it change how places are left? What would you add, and what's been a waste of time?

Disclosure: I'm building a digital welcome book for hosts, so I'm genuinely trying to learn what hosts value. I'm not linking it here, but happy to answer if anyone asks.

replies.text: That's a great one, thanks. Did you notice a difference straight away, or more over a season?

replies.when: A frustrated "what do we do now?" thread
replies.text: Totally get it. It's your place and you want it looked after. One thing that helps, whatever the platforms allow: tell guests who you are and how the house works. "Collection is Wednesday, yellow lid is recycling" isn't a rule, it's information, and most people are happy to help once they know whose home it is.

replies.when: "What should I put in my welcome?"
replies.text: I'd keep it to five things: who you are (a name and a line about why you love the place), a bit of the home's story, how the tricky things work (hot water, the sticky door), bin day and which bin is which, and your favourite local spots. Write it like you'd tell a friend staying over, not like a list of rules.

replies.when: Someone asks for tools or apps (only where the group allows it)
replies.text: Full disclosure, I built one, so I'm biased: DigiStayBook puts your welcome, the house info and a guestbook behind a QR code. Happy to answer questions, and plenty of hosts do just fine with a well-written printed folder too.

campaign.title: A home with a host
campaign.line: Let guests see the care. Give them a clear way to care for it.
campaign.audience: Australian owner-hosts of one or a few cottages, cabins and holiday homes who care about the place and want their welcome to sound like them.
campaign.promise: Your welcome, your house guidance and your own memory wall, in a browser guests can open from your property QR display.
campaign.rationale: Lead with the person and the home, then offer useful wording, then show the product. Respect is the aim; clear guidance and a recognisable host are the mechanisms we can actually demonstrate.
campaign.conversion: Primary action: explore the guest demo. Next action: create an account and add one property with a welcome note and one practical house essential. Do not make an unverified time-to-setup or outcome promise.
campaign.scope: Original campaign developed from local product source and current local demo captures. No internet research, competitor documents or online marketing documents consulted. Suggested dates only; nothing is published or scheduled.

operations.cadence: Five Facebook feed posts (including one Reel), seven lightweight Stories, five Pinterest Pins, and two optional TikTok exports. Thursday and Saturday are Facebook feed rest days. Daily Stories are optional if capacity is tight.
channelRoles: Longer host-first captions, one multi-image writing lesson, one actual product Reel, one open question and one worksheet. Use the Page feed; no group posting or outreach is included.
Searchable titles, vertical writing guides and checklists, each with its own destination. Treat the first month as a catalogue-building experiment; no instant traffic promise.
Two captioned 9:16 exports with different hooks. Account not yet established. No TikTok-specific performance claim or dependency in the main plan.
operations.timing: Suggested test slots in Sydney time: Facebook feed 7:30 pm; Stories 8:00 am; Pinterest 8:30 pm. These are practical starting slots, not researched best times. Leave TikTok unscheduled until the account and profile destination are ready.
operations.budget: Organic-first. No paid spend, publishing, scheduling, outreach or account creation included.
operations.measurement: Maintain a simple dated log per creative: published URL, impressions/reach, useful host comments, saves, outbound clicks, and attributable account/property setup where tracking actually exists. Use UTM links; do not assume the full setup funnel is instrumented.
operations.hypothesis: Working creative hypothesis, not a forecast: host recognition earns attention; useful wording earns saves; real product demonstrations earn demo visits.
operations.decision: At the end of week one, choose the next two pieces using the strongest useful signal: real host questions, saves and demo clicks. Expand a useful topic into a new example and layout; do not clone the top-performing image. Low response is a reason to test the hook or destination, not proof that the product does not work.
operations.outcome: Desired month-end evidence: identifiable host needs, people exploring the demo, and hosts trying a first-property welcome. No claim that post engagement demonstrates more respectful guest behaviour.

facebook.title: Your first welcome, in three lines
facebook.caption:
Try this before you add another house rule.

Write three short lines:
1. “Welcome to…” — the feeling you want guests to have.
2. “One thing we love about this home…” — a detail only you could share.
3. “Please help us look after…” — one clear request, with a reason.

For example:
“Welcome to our little garden cottage. We planted the herb beds during our first winter here. Please snip a few leaves for dinner and leave the roots growing for the next guests.”

That is example copy, not a customer story. Keep the welcome brief, then put practical instructions in your house essentials and host notes.
